Information of citizenship, even if inferred, has been documented since before 1870. ONLY TWICE was that question not asked since it began; once in 1960 and once in 2010.

Data about place of birth can suggest citizenship, and effectively more so when it includes parents. To be clear, the place of birth itself DOES NOT indicate citizenship, but is related to several laws regarding citizenship. There has been a specific citizenship question for quite a long time. Data about language could also be considered relevant to immigration and integration, which can also suggest citizenship. Interestingly, There were no questions about language or literacy in 1950. The census wasn't always taken the same way. In the 1800's, there was data gathered separately for Native Indians, slaves and free colored persons.

The official source of info for the census questions is https://www.census.gov The PDFs aren't small, so click the links with patience. In particular, let's take a look at questions relating to place of birth, language and citizenship. For perspective, let's also look at a few other major events in the timeline.

1783 - American Revolutionary War ends. US census begins in 1790.

1840 and previous - No questions about place of birth, language or citizenship. The census was little more than a head count for an area.

1850 - Place of birth: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1850_questionnaire.pdf

1860 - Place of birth: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/frederickdouglass1860.pdf

1870 - Place of birth, parents foreign-born or not, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/emilydickinson1870.pdf

1880 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1880_questionnaire.pdf

1890 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1890_questionnaire.pdf

1900 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1900_questionnaire.pdf

1910 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, spoken language, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1910_questionnaire.pdf

1918 - World War 1 ends (1914-1918)

1920 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, native language, parents native language, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1920_questionnaire.pdf

1924 - Immigration Act passed: https://history.house.gov/Historical-Highlights/1901-1950/The-Immigration-Act-of-1924/

1930 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, native language, English literacy: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1930questionnaire-102018.pdf

1940 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, native language: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1940_population_questionnaire.pdf

1945 - World War 2 Ends (1939-1945)

1950 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1950_population_questionnaire.pdf

1953 - Korean War ends (1950-1953)

1960 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, previous language if foreign: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1960censusquestionnaire-2.pdf

1965 - Immigration and Nationality Act passed. This ended the restrictions of how many immigrants allowed: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-79/pdf/STATUTE-79-Pg911.pdf

1970 - Place of birth, parents place of birth, citizenship, previous language if foreign: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1970_questionnaire.pdf

1975 - Vietnam war ends (1955-1975)

1980 - Place of birth, citizenship, other language and English fluency: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1980_long_questionnaire.pdf

1990 - Place of birth, citizenship, other language and English fluency: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/1990_questionnaire.pdf

1990 - Kennedy's Immigration Act passed: https://www.congress.gov/bill/101st-congress/senate-bill/358

2000 - Place of birth, citizenship, other language and English fluency: https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/2000_long_form.pdf

2010 - No place of birth questions. No citizenship questions. No language questions. Actually, it had only 10 questions. This was the smallest and least informative census the US had in well over 100 years. https://www.census.gov/history/pdf/2010questionnaire.pdf

2020 - TBD. A plan to count non-responders us also currently under development: https://www.census.gov/2019censustest
